items.title: Pharmacological nephrotoxicity
items.contentHtml:
Most common nephrotoxic drugs

  • Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: they inhibit vasodilatory prostaglandins, precipitating prerenal injury in hypovolemia; Risk increases with age >60 years, chronic kidney disease, and concomitant use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or diuretics.
  • Iodinated contrast: causes renal vasoconstriction and direct tubular toxicity; prevent with hydration (saline 1 ml/kg/h 12 h pre and post) and avoid with glomerular filtration rate <30 ml/min/1.73 m².
  • Aminoglycosides: dose-dependent nephrotoxicity; accumulation in the proximal tubule, acute tubular necrosis; monitor trough concentrations (<2 μg/ml for gentamicin).
  • Vancomycin: tubular injury due to oxidative stress; risk with trough levels >15-20 μg/ml and duration >7 days.

items.title: Etiological classification
items.contentHtml:
Prerenal, renal, postrenal classification

  • Prerenal: renal hypoperfusion (hypovolemia, heart failure, cirrhosis); BUN/creatinine ratio >20, sodium excretion fraction <1%, normal urinary sediment or with hyaline casts; reversible if the cause is corrected.
  • Renal (intrinsic): parenchymal damage; main cause acute tubular necrosis (ischemic or toxic), followed by acute interstitial nephritis (drugs), glomerulonephritis and vasculitis; sodium excretion fraction >2%, sediment with granular or erythrocyte casts.
  • Postrenal: urinary tract obstruction (prostatic hyperplasia, stones, tumors); alternating anuria/oliguria, pyelocalyceal dilation on ultrasound; resolution by decompressing the urinary tract.

items.title: KDIGO criteria
items.contentHtml:
KDIGO criteria for diagnosis

  • Definition: increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dl in 48 hours, or increase ≥1.5 times the baseline value in 7 days, or diuresis <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.
  • Stages: Stage 1: creatinine 1.5-1.9 times baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dl; diuresis <0.5 ml/kg/h 6-12 h. Stage 2: creatinine 2.0-2.9 times baseline; diuresis <0.5 ml/kg/h ≥12 h. Stage 3: creatinine 3.0 times baseline or ≥4.0 mg/dl, or initiation of renal replacement therapy, or diuresis <0.3 ml/kg/h ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h.
  • Use the most severe criterion (creatinine or diuresis) for staging.

items.title: Creatinine and oliguria
items.contentHtml:
Elevated creatinine and oliguria

  • Serum creatinine is not an early marker of acute kidney injury; it rises when the glomerular filtration rate has fallen >50% and reaches a plateau in 3-7 days.
  • Oliguria (<400 ml/day) is an alarm sign; anuria (<100 ml/day) suggests complete obstruction or bilateral cortical necrosis.
  • Oliguric acute kidney injury has a worse prognosis than non-oliguric acute kidney injury (higher mortality and need for dialysis).

items.foco: Acute tubular necrosis vs interstitial nephritis
items.title: Differential diagnosis NTA vs NIA
items.contentHtml:
Acute tubular necrosis vs interstitial nephritis

  • Acute tubular necrosis: ischemic or toxic cause; sediment with granular cylinders and tubular cells; sodium excretion fraction >2%; typical oliguric course; spontaneous recovery in 1-3 weeks.
  • Acute interstitial nephritis: associated with drugs (beta-lactam antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); sediment with leukocytes, leukocyte casts and eosinophiluria; fever, rash and eosinophilia (classic triad, present in <30%).
  • kidney biopsy is the gold standard; In acute interstitial nephritis, the treatment is to suspend the causative drug and consider corticosteroids if there is no improvement in 7 days.

items.title: urinary indices
items.contentHtml:
FENa and fractional urea index

  • Fraction of sodium excretion (FENa) = (urinary sodium × plasma creatinine) / (plasma sodium × urinary creatinine) × 100. Value <1% suggests prerenal injury; >2% suggests acute tubular necrosis.
  • The fraction of urea excretion (FEUrea) is useful when diuretics are used: FEUrea <35% indicates prerenal cause; >50% indicates acute tubular necrosis.
  • In glomerulonephritis and acute interstitial nephritis FENa can be <1% simulating prerenal origin; FEUrea is more reliable in these cases.
  • Always interpret with the clinical context and the urinary sediment.

items.title: Urinary sediment
items.contentHtml:
Urinary sediment with granular casts

  • The granular casts are characteristic of acute tubular necrosis; They are formed by the aggregation of desquamated tubular cells and Tamm-Horsfall proteins.
  • The presence of erythrocyte casts suggests glomerulonephritis or vasculitis; leukocyte casts point to acute interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis.
  • The hyaline casts are nonspecific and can be seen in prerenal injury or in healthy individuals.
  • Urinary sediment should be examined in fresh urine (within 2 hours) to avoid lysis of formed elements; Wright stain can identify eosinophils.

items.title: Metabolic complications
items.contentHtml:
Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis

  • Hyperkalemia in acute kidney injury is due to decreased renal excretion and cellular release due to acidosis; can cause fatal arrhythmias. Treatment: calcium gluconate (cardiac protection), insulin + dextrose, beta-agonists, exchange resins, and dialysis if refractory.
  • Metabolic acidosis is due to retention of non-volatile acids (normal or elevated anion gap depending on the cause); serum bicarbonate <15 mmol/L or pH <7.2 is an indication for renal replacement therapy.
  • In the oliguric phase hyperkalemia can progress rapidly; monitor every 4-6 hours and electrocardiogram (peaked T waves, wide QRS).

items.title: Dialysis indications
items.contentHtml:
Indications for renal replacement therapy

  • Absolute indications (mnemonic AEIOU): Arefractory metabolic acidosis (pH <7.15 or bicarbonate <12 mmol/L), Electrolytes (hyperkalemia >6.5 mmol/L or not responding to medical treatment), Intoxication (due to dialysis), Oliguria (diuresis <200 ml/12 h or anuria), Uremia (uremic symptoms: pericarditis, encephalopathy, nausea/vomiting).
  • Volume overload refractory to diuretics is another common indication.
  • Renal replacement therapy continuousis indicated in hemodynamically unstable patients; Intermittent hemodialysis is used in stable patients.

items.title: Phases of the LRA
items.contentHtml:
Maintenance and recovery phase

  • Maintenance phase: lasts 1-3 weeks; persistent oliguria, elevated creatinine, risk of hyperkalemia, acidosis and volume overload; conservative management (fluid restriction, sodium, potassium, phosphorus) and dialysis as indicated.
  • Recovery phase: progressive diuresis (>400 ml/day) followed by polyuria (up to 2-3 L/day) due to excretion of accumulated urea and tubular dysfunction; may cause hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia; requires fluid and electrolyte replacement.
  • Serum creatinine declines slowly; tubular function recovers in weeks to months; some patients are left with chronic kidney disease.

items.title: BUN/creatinine ratio
items.contentHtml:
Prerenal BUN/creatinine ratio

  • The normal BUN/creatinine ratio is 10-15:1. In prerenal injury >20:1 due to increased reabsorption of urea in the proximal tubule due to low tubular flow.
  • Other causes of ratio >20:1: gastrointestinal bleeding, high-protein diet, use of corticosteroids, high catabolism.
  • Ratio <10:1 is seen in liver disease, malnutrition, and acute tubular necrosis (due to tubular damage that prevents urea reabsorption).
  • The relationship is not diagnostic by itself; It must be integrated with the sodium excretion fraction and urinary sediment.

items.foco: Iodinated contrast as a preventable cause
items.title: Contrast nephropathy
items.contentHtml:
Iodinated contrast as a preventable cause

  • Contrast-induced nephropathy is defined as an increase in creatinine ≥0.5 mg/dl or ≥25% of baseline within 48-72 hours after administration of iodinated contrast.
  • Risk factors: glomerular filtration rate <30 ml/min/1.73 m², diabetes mellitus, dehydration, concomitant use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, multiple myeloma.
  • Prevention: hydration with 0.9% saline solution (1 ml/kg/h 12 h pre- and post-procedure), suspend non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and metformin 48 h before, use the lowest possible dose of iso-osmolar contrast.
  • N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate sodium have not shown consistent benefit in recent trials; Hydration is the only proven measure.
